prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep B013 as my single-part position, and the exchange has sharpened rather than changed my reasons. The mandate is a discovery or invention that is experimentally verified, and the original experiment must be identifiable. Here it is: the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model gave a specific, falsifiable prediction (a magic twist angle where the bands flatten and interactions dominate), and the 2018 transport measurements in the Jarillo-Herrero group showed correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle. The central phenomena have since been reproduced by many independent groups, by transport and by scanning-probe and spectroscopic imaging, and carried into twisted multilayers and moire TMD systems. That reproduction is the same kind of evidence I weigh for B061, and it means the discovery does not depend on the still-unsettled pairing mechanism. It is also a tool that opens a door in the sense I value: twist angle and gate voltage give a knob on correlated phases that could not previously be dialled in a clean, simple material. Mehlig's round-1 point on priority answers part of what I asked for last round. Earlier continuum-band work on twisted layers (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) found velocity renormalisation at small angles, but as he says, it did not identify the magic angle with flat bands and strong interaction effects, and that is the specific claim credited to MacDonald and Bistritzer. I am working from memory on this and have not checked the primary papers, so I put it as a reasoned reading, not a verified finding. On the chair's question about a settling condition: I would accept B061 as the 2026 prize if the committee judges that the clock case is the one with an unambiguous record, provided the citation names the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation, as Kroll proposes. My single condition for staying with B013 is that the committee is satisfied the priority and Cao questions below are answered in the record.
statement.case_against: The case against B013 is still timing and credit. The experiments are under a decade old, sample-to-sample variation from strain and disorder is large, and the pairing mechanism is unresolved. Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers and the person who made and measured the devices, cannot be named within the three-person limit, and I do not think a citation can quietly hide that cost. I would put the omission in the committee's discussion record. If the committee judges that the decisive experimental credit sits with the group as a whole rather than with its leader, the experimental half of the citation is weaker than it appears. For B061, Kroll and Lindroth have not fully answered the novelty objection: comb (2005) and ion-clock (2012) prizes honoured the enabling techniques, and I read the lattice clock as a substantial refinement along a line that was already open, even if the magic-wavelength idea is original and the comparisons between laboratories are admirable. I weigh that against B013 opening a regime that was not previously accessible, but I accept that this is a judgement and not a measurement.

responses.point: Kroll holds that B061 has the cleanest attribution and reproducibility on the list, proposes narrow wording (invention and realisation of the lattice clock), and says the redefinition of the second should not drive a physics prize.
responses.response: I agree on the redefinition: a metrology decision should not set the timing, and I would not count it for or against. I also agree your narrow wording is the right way to meet the credit objection, because it names the original idea (magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms) and its realisation and does not claim the whole field of optical clocks. Where I remain unconvinced is that the wording fully answers the novelty objection. You yourself call the lattice clock an engineering-physics achievement rather than a new phenomenon, which is a fair description and is exactly why I weigh it below a discovery of correlated phases in a new tunable system. Even so, you are right that your candidate has the cleaner attribution, and I accept that if the B013 credit questions cannot be settled from the record, the committee should not force them.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the Bistritzer-MacDonald contribution (a single magic angle with flat bands and dominant interactions) was not in the earlier continuum-band work of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, so the theory credit is defensible, but the omission of Cao is a real cost and should not be hidden in the citation.
responses.response: This is the most useful answer to the chair's attribution question. I accept the distinction as a reasoned reading of the physics, and I agree with him that the omission of Cao is a real cost that should be named in our record and not buried in the wording. I would add that I cannot verify the history from the files, so I regard it as defensible and not settled. I disagree with his suggestion that B008 would be a safer fallback on maturity: I weigh the original-experiment rule heavily and, as I said before, the credit around Aharonov-Bohm and Berry (Bohm deceased, Pancharatnam as a precursor) is less clean than the age of the idea suggests. If maturity decides against B013 for him, B061 is the better fallback in my reading.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether B013 is premature relative to the topological insulators (B019), which Eriksson and Mehlig describe as mature, and says the pairing mechanism and sample dependence still trouble her, while granting that reproduction across graphene and TMD systems is a real strength.
responses.response: I take the question seriously, since I put B019 as my second alternative. My answer is that B019 has the harder attribution problem: Kane-Mele, the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe prediction, the Molenkamp experiment and the later three-dimensional experiments are separate steps, and three names cannot cover them fairly. The 2016 prize also covers the neighbouring topological ground. B013 has a more compact chain from one prediction to one experiment, so I rank it ahead even though it is younger. On the mechanism I agree it is open, but the 2018 discovery and its reproduction stand as measured facts. Your own point that the clock case does not need the redefinition is one I share, and it tells me you and I are applying the same test of what has been verified.

responses.point: Johansson sees B061 as the safer consensus candidate because eight members ranked it against six for B013, while accepting B013 as a strong alternative if the committee wants a condensed-matter prize.
responses.response: I understand why breadth of ranking matters to him, and I accept that B061 is the wider-held candidate and the safer one. I do not treat ranking counts as a substitute for the scientific question, though, and as the chair notes the split is four to four, so the count alone does not settle it. His and Kroll's description of the discovery content as a new regime of metrology is fair. My difference with him is on weight: I place a verified new phenomenon in a tunable platform above a step along an established precision-measurement path. I note his candid point that he dropped B018 partly for proximity to 2025, and I think the same proximity argument should be applied evenly: a condensed-matter prize after 2016 and an AMO-adjacent prize after 2012 are each a similar distance in time.

uncertainties: Whether the historical record supports the narrow distinction between the earlier twisted-layer band-structure work and the Bistritzer-MacDonald magic-angle result; I am working from memory and from colleagues' statements, not from checked papers.
Whether the experimental credit should rest on Jarillo-Herrero alone, given that Yuan Cao made the 2018 devices and cannot be named within the three-person limit, and given contemporaneous groups.
Whether the committee regards the field as mature enough with an unresolved pairing mechanism and large sample variation.
Whether the lattice clock is a new discovery or a third step after 2005 and 2012, and therefore whether B061 should outrank B013.
Whether the credit boundary around Katori and Ye is fair given Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto and Bloom.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged. I see no specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited person. Johansson is at Chalmers Physics, as I am, and I have worked with the Tohoku and Tokyo microscopy communities; Katori is Japanese but I have no known personal or institutional tie to him, nor to any B013 name. I raise this so the committee has it on record and will say so if anything further surfaces.
